pr_title: Asyncronously pull images while init container is running

**What type of PR is this?**
/kind feature

**What this PR does / why we need it**:

The aim here is to optimize the startup process for a pod with an initContainer (or multiple) followed by a set of normal containers as discussed in #88265.

Currently the initContainer pulls it's image, runs for a while, then after exiting the normal containers images are pulled (if not present) and the containers started. Note if you have multiple initContainers this flow is repeated with init1 pull-> run then init 2 pull -> run then main workload.

This PR moves to pulling all the required images asynchronously while the first init container is running. 

With this change in place startup times for pods with images not already on the nodes are significantly improved. Here are tests run with this change tracking timings: https://github.com/lawrencegripper/hack-testingasyncpull#results-with-ordered-async

My vague recollection of image pulling is that if you pull the same image twice, both calls should return after the first call returns.  I wonder if we can just "fire and forget" the initial async image pull call for containers, and still get the benefit?  That would probably reduce much of the complexity this adds, as we don't have to track individual image pull calls.

My main concern with this change would be that it could cause disk I/O contention.  Do you know if we currently pull images serially or in parallel when creating + starting containers today?  I don't remember off the top of my head.  If we are already pulling them in parallel, this probably isn't a big concern.

> @mattjmcnaughton Thanks for taking a look, totally agree about the added code complexity. I set out thinking this would be a very minor change and am very conscious of it being on the critical path for pod creation. In terms of how the change translates to calls to the `ImageService` it should (I hope) not result in any additional calls either to `PulImage` or `GetImageRef` (although I'm not convinced the number of these calls matters too much).
> 
> @dashpole yeah my early testing with docker suggested that this is the case and identical image pull requests are deduped by docker. Discussion here: [#88265 (comment)](https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/88265#issuecomment-588161338) (downside is imagepullbackoff wouldn't be tracked if async pull failed but maybe could work around this somehow). If this is acceptable we can rip out quite a bit of this code and simplify, this feels like a good option to me. Regarding disk contention the change would respect the current settings for the cluster. There is currently an option for either serial or parallel image pulling set here: https://github.com/lawrencegripper/kubernetes/blob/ed5bb06/cmd/kubelet/app/options/options.go#L546
> 
> I'd love more data to be able to answer if the improvements hold for more general use cases. My gut feeling is that this does only help in a single circumstance (you have an init container and large images).
> 
> The scenario driving this change was when a new node is brought up by the autoscaler how quickly can it start running a required pod, specifically around GPU based models. This change sped things up as those Pods have an init container configured and a relatively large image size for the main pod image - this is where things get a bit unknown for me in terms of improvement for users in wider context.
> 
> The team I worked with had an init container followed by a large image for the main container so they would see around a 30second improvement in time from the pod being assigned to the node to running the main containers with this change. Specifically, for them they're using a CRON schedule to start work at a specific time and want to minimize the delay between the CRON firing and the computation starting. In their business context this time saving is of a high value.
> 
> In terms of the alternatives for achieving something similar and pre-pulling required image sooner a daemon set could be used with all the required images specified so that all machines in the cluster start pulling the images when they are started. Although this was a bit of a blunt instrument as all images would be pulled on all nodes and they're large.

Thanks for your thoughtful responses - what do you view as the next steps from here @lawrencegripper ?

So I guess there are three options:

1. Take it forward as is. Con: high complexity to optimize specific use-case
2. Simplify by relying on container runtime to deduplicate pulls. Pro: Much simpler change Con: Pull errors for async pulls not tracked for imagepullbackoff
3. Don't take it forward as trade-offs don't make sense. 

In terms of next steps I'm happy to code up option 2 and we can then compare the three options. Sound like a good plan?

Also happy to close this one out if consensus is around option 3.

Just to confirm, is this an accurate description of option #2 ?
1. We fire the pulls as soon as the init container starts, but don't do any tracking around if they are successful.
2. When actually trying to run the containers, we will see if the images exist. If yes, we are done. If the images don't exist, because the async pull was unsuccessful, we will then retry pulling them, this time with all of the image pullbackoff. **My one question is what happens if the image pull is still in progress when the init containers are done? Specifically, what if it is in-progress when the init containers are done, and then the in-progress pull fails.**

Re moving forward, if you are comfortable implementing option #2 , I'd certainly be interested to see what that implementation looks like. I can't necessarily guarantee it'd be merged though (that's an OWNERs call to make :) ). So up to you - I definitely want to be respectful of your time and investment!

> @mattjmcnaughton:
> I'm having trouble parsing the exact impact we expect this to have. At a high level, I'm curious to know in what scenarios users will notice these improvements, and how large the improvements will be.

Our use-case is: we do e2e testing with minikube, a massive "distributed monolith" with some ~30 services with up to 1-6 init containers each, totaling around 50 unique image pulls on each PR run. Some of the init containers just wait for other services to start in order to control the startup order.

Would be nice to "pre-pull" everything at the start and save some time. Right now there's a lot of inefficient waiting for images to be pulled very late when they could've been pulled earlier.

For reference, it takes around 30 minutes for us to boot up the environment on a cold 32-core 128GB runner. I'm guesstimating that time could be cut in half if all images were pre-pulled at the beginning.

issue_context.title: Pull main pods images while int container executing
comments: w.r.t. the de-duplication of the calls to EnsureImagePresent, the ImageManager needs to expose the images currently being downloaded so that, if init container runs to completion before the download is finished, we can wait on the image download instead of launching another download.

We should also consider if this feature would be conditionally enabled.
For init container whose image is small and whose execution is fast, the savings in async image download are not much.
Maybe we can get statistics from the first few init container runs along with duration for normal container image download so that we can decide whether to enable the async image download.

Sounds like a good plan, with regard to the statistics is there a source of these I can pull from or is it best to run some test scenarios on a cluster? 

For scenarios I'm thinking about testing with `x` initContainer's which run for for `y` secs with images of `z` size. I can then calculate the potential time savings for various values of `x/y/z` and get some more clear metrics of at which point this becomes useful and how useful it is in terms of time savings. 

For de-duplication of `EnsureImagePresent` I've had a bit of a play locally with the docker daemon and found that it's already going to do this for us without any additional code. In the two recordings below I run a `docker pull`x2 on the same image at the same time and another where I start one of the pulls 10 seconds after the first. Both appear to result in the daemon only doing one pull with the later call reporting the context of the already in-progress pull. My assumption is the daemon uses a locking mechanism to ensure only one instance of a pull in progress for the same image. I'm a little unclear on what tests would be needed on different container runtimes, any ideas? 

![dockerdaemonpullsync1](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1939288/74828012-43c34000-5306-11ea-95fd-e5c366190f87.gif)

![dockerdaemonpullsync2](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/1939288/74828009-42921300-5306-11ea-8adf-4194936acd93.gif)

Woops, yeah as I wasn't receiving from the `pullChan` so the hacky version would block the puller. For testing now I'm just using a go routine in the async version to make sure the result it received. Will look at doing something better if the stats show the changes to prepull is worthwhile. 

>How do you check for the completion of prepulling image(s) ?

As I mentioned above it looks like the docker daemon is handling the de-duplication of the pull requests so I wasn't planning to track the results of the `EnsureImageExistsAsync` calls as when the normal `start` func is called for the containers the result of `EnsureImageExists` will return the progress of the already submitted pull request (need to test more). Sound reasonable? Happy to look at doing something more complex to track them if that is preferred.
